idiom_name: ABC with @abstractmethod sandbox method and single-underscore primitives (BaseHTTPRequestHandler shape)
implementation_notes: Python has no access control, so the sandbox wall is the single-underscore convention plus documentation, and abc.ABC with @abstractmethod enforces only the sandbox method - and only at instantiation time. The standard library shows the pattern's real-world shape in http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler: a subclass implements do_GET (and do_HEAD/do_POST) and composes the response from the provided operations send_response, send_header, end_headers and the wfile attribute, never touching the socket. Name mangling is not a substitute for protected: an identifier of the form __primitive is rewritten to _Class__primitive, so it stays reachable from outside and an override written as __primitive in a subclass mangles to a different name and is never called. What replaces the classic structure where behaviours hold no state is a sandbox object or a small protocol of callables passed into plain functions; the ABC form stays the clearest when a framework drives the family and behaviours keep state.
pitfalls: abc enforcement happens when a class is instantiated, not when it is defined: a behaviour that forgot the sandbox method fails only if something constructs it, so tests must instantiate every concrete behaviour.

Name mangling is not privacy: _Power__play_sound is reachable from anywhere, and a subclass that overrides __play_sound by the same spelling creates _Sub__play_sound while the base keeps calling the mangled base name, so the override silently never runs.
typing.final is a static-type-checker promise only; a subclass can still replace a primitive or the entry method at run time.
Calling the sandbox method from __init__ dispatches before the subclass has initialised its own attributes, which shows up as AttributeError at construction time.
